memories.memory_text: I was thrown into a chair and backhanded so hard I hit the floor—my nose broke, I tasted blood, and then I saw that cloaked figure in the dark.

After they hit me again, I spat out a tooth and tried to deflect with a joke about play genres—but then another blow came, and I saw laughing faces that weren’t there, flashing in my mind before I was back in the room, bleeding.
I woke to the door crashing open and a guard shouting my name—then a parchment slapped into my lap, saying I was free. I just stared at it, not understanding how or why.
Oxford had his servant give me a leather-bound manuscript and told me to stage it under my name. Then he said I was to put my name to all his plays, not just this one.
I stood there clutching the pouch of coins, the weight of it cold and shameful, and when I looked up, they were gone—Oxford vanished, Francesco gone, and I couldn't even find the way out of the maze.
I remember the way Nashe slurred his words, boasting that writing in iambic pentameter wasn’t hard—like it meant nothing. I had to ask him, coldly, if he’d ever even tried.
I turned and looked at Kit, really looked at him, after he lied to my face about the arrest—like I wouldn’t know the stink of betrayal when I smell it—and then I just walked away.

I was walking with a whore, a bit unsteady on my feet, when I saw a crowd near the Mermaid—someone said a body, and when they turned him over, it was Marlowe, a wound in his eye, dried blood like a black star. I couldn’t speak, couldn’t move—Marlowe, dead in an alley like a common thief.

I stood by the stand, ale in hand, watching the crowd—then Francesco came, handed me a leather folder and a purse that jingled. I took them without counting, feeling the weight of it, and walked away fast, not looking back.

I saw him unroll that gaudy coat-of-arms, all bright colors and foolish symbols—like a man buying his way into a world he never earned. When he said 'Not without right?' I snapped—'Right!? Not without right?'—because I knew he’d gone to that man, broken my word, lied to me.

I shoved the parchment at him, thrust the quill in his face—'Go on, Will. Write something for us. Now.' I mocked him, dared him to prove he was still a writer, not just some gentleman in velvet—but he just stood there, said I had no ink, then walked out.

I saw Condell on stage, limping and hunched, playing 'Gloucester'—it was unmistakably Cecil, twisted and mocked in front of everyone. The lines about being deformed and barked at by dogs... they cut too close.
Burbage told me—no Jonson plays at the Globe. Ever. I still felt the weight of my manuscript in my hand, and that grin I’d worn just froze, then broke.
I walked the streets in the rain, alone, and saw the Tower of London. I made a decision.

I sat in that chair, the same one Marlowe had been in, and I hated myself for it—rain on the windows, Pole staring at me, waiting. I told him about the play, Shakespeare's Richard the Third, how it showed a king murdered, the throne stolen, and the killer played as a hunchback.

I stood at the edge of the galleries, biting my nails, watching the groundlings file in, and when Dekker said they were waiting, I snapped—'Waiting? Waiting for what?'—because I knew it wasn't just about the play anymore.
I saw the crowd turn on the stage the moment Gloucester appeared—they weren’t just watching a play, they were hissing at Cecil himself, and the actor could barely speak over the noise.
Oxford’s box was empty, and then I saw Francesco down there with the groundlings—something felt wrong, like they were hiding in plain sight.

I saw it then—the way Oxford was using the play, how 'Up with Essex!' wasn't just a line, it was a signal. This wasn't theater anymore; they were rallying a mob, and Essex was waiting for exactly this.

I had to get to Francesco, had to warn Cecil—'He already knows,' I thought, but still I ran. The crowd pulled me like a current, and I could barely move, but I knew I had to act before it was too late.
I was near Francesco in the thick of the crowd on the bridge when the soldiers yanked down the tarps and revealed the cannons—then the officer shouted 'Fire!' and everything exploded into chaos.
I saw Francesco fall, the pike piercing him as he shouted at me to run—I just stood there, frozen, the crowd surging around me.
I charged at Will with my sword, shouting he was a fraud and a murderer. The actors watched, nervous.
He grabbed me by the throat, face to face, and said, 'You came to me, Ben,' then shoved me down—I remember the shock of it, the silence after the fall.

I remember standing there as Anne demanded I leave, her voice sharp with distrust, and how the second doctor appeared just in time, saying, 'He's asking for you,'—those words parting the air like a reprieve.
I remember the weight of his gaze when he asked what I truly thought of his work—how my voice nearly failed me before I whispered that his words were the most wondrous ever heard on any stage.

I remember the pile of manuscripts by his bed, the way he nodded to them and told me to keep them safe—from his family, from the Cecils—and to wait before publishing, as if I were being handed a secret too heavy to carry.
I walked out of Oxford's room with the manuscripts under my arm, my hands unsteady, heart still pounding from what I'd just witnessed inside.
Anne screamed at me to get out, called the theaters blasphemous—but I turned and told her none of them would be remembered without Oxford’s art. Then I walked away.

I was walking away, reading the dedication—'To the Earl of Southampton'—and then it hit me, standing there, that Oxford’s work wasn’t just words on a page; there was something beneath it, some hidden design I couldn’t name, and I froze, staring back at the house, suddenly unsure of everything I thought I knew.
I told Cecil the manuscripts were burned by his own men—I could see the doubt in his eyes, but I had to protect Oxford, even if it meant lying to save what he left behind.
Cecil told me to wipe Oxford's memory for all time. I stared at him and said, 'I am afraid that this is not possible, my lord.' He smiled, then left.
I found the metal box in the ashes, pried it open with my hands, and saw the manuscripts inside—singed but whole. When I saw the pages survived, I couldn’t help but smile, relief washing over me.
I wrote the dedication to his works—Shakespeare’s—knowing full well the weight of it, though he was gone and I remained, the first Poet Laureate, the most celebrated playwright of my time.

Ruin? Dishonor? Madam. You, your family, me, even Elizabeth herself shall be remembered solely because we had the honor to live whilst your husband put ink to paper.
A command performance for our new king! Even in bloody Scotland they've heard of bloody Will Shakespeare, have they? Fraud. Charlatan. Counterfeiter of wit! Murderer!
He was something I could never be. An undeniable perfection... that plagued my soul... And to him I was... nothing. A messenger. Nothing more.

I find... your words... the most
wondrous ever heard on our stage. On
any stage... Ever.
Plays? Which would you prefer, my lord? pastoral? An historical? An historical-pastoral, or an hysterical historical pastoral--
To the Earl of Southampton. The love I dedicate to your lordship is without end; whereof this pamphlet, without beginning, is but a superfluous moiety.

Not half--?! You're an actor, what in God's name do you know about writing?! He's an amateur, Will, a complete and utter amateur. Last week gardening, this week playwrighting, next week hawking. (takes another swig) No. I won't do it. It would be an affront against the Muses...
I tell you Will-- I came to London to become a great poet, to, to, be the conscience of our times, the soul of our age! To change the world, not to become someone else's--
Right!? Not without right? (beat) You went to him, didn't you? You lying knave-- you went to him!

relations.relation_summary: The relationship between Ben Jonson and Oxford is complex, characterized by a deep literary collaboration intertwined with emotional tension and conflicting motivations. Social relationship evidence reveals a multifaceted bond: Oxford acts as a mentor and patron, recognizing Jonson's talent and actively supporting his career, including securing his release from imprisonment and aiming to elevate his status as a playwright. This supportive dynamic is reinforced by Oxford providing Jonson with manuscripts and inviting him to collaborate on staging plays, using Jonson's name to shield Oxford's own identity as the true author. Jonson, in turn, expresses profound admiration for Oxford, calling his words 'the most wondrous ever heard' and referring to him as 'the soul of the age,' indicating deep intellectual respect and emotional reverence. However, this affinity is counterbalanced by overt hostility—Oxford confronts Jonson with anger when he feels his intentions are misunderstood, particularly regarding the attribution of plays, revealing a power struggle and personal friction. Key joint events underscore this duality: while they share intense moments of eye contact and enter the garden maze together, symbolizing a moment of connection, other interactions are charged with control and resistance, such as when Oxford insists Jonson claim authorship of all his plays, and when Jonson mimics Oxford’s mannerisms while asserting his own ambitions, suggesting both influence and rebellion. Their collaboration is thus marked by mutual dependence—Oxford needs Jonson as a public front, and Jonson gains opportunity through Oxford’s patronage—yet strained by ego, pride, and conflicting visions. The relationship evolves from one-sided mentorship toward a more contested alliance, where admiration coexists with resentment, ultimately shaping both characters’ artistic and personal trajectories.

The relationship between Ben Jonson and Marlowe is defined by deep-seated hostility, mutual accusations of betrayal, and a competitive professional rivalry. Social relationship evidence reveals that Jonson holds Marlowe responsible for informing on him to the Tower, resulting in his arrest—an act Jonson perceives as a profound betrayal, especially given their shared circle. This accusation triggers hostile confrontations, with Marlowe responding with lies and threats, further escalating tensions. Their rivalry is also intellectual and artistic, as seen in Marlowe's sarcastic challenges to Jonson's authorship claims, particularly regarding historical dramas, indicating a competitive dynamic rooted in professional pride and envy. Events they share underscore this antagonism: Marlowe interrupts Jonson’s work uninvited, asserting dominance or intrusion, while Jonson flees from Marlowe in a moment of physical tension, suggesting fear or avoidance. Marlowe attempts to manipulate Jonson by offering anonymity for secrets—a transactional overture that implies distrust and exploitation. The climax of their relationship occurs when Jonson discovers Marlowe’s body in an alley, a moment that may carry emotional weight, though the nature of his reaction (grief, relief, or ambivalence) is not specified. This final event closes their narrative arc without evidence of reconciliation, leaving their relationship unresolved and marked by conflict. The emotional dynamics are consistently charged with suspicion, resentment, and power struggles, influencing both characters’ actions—Jonson’s defensiveness and Marlowe’s manipulative persistence. The relationship does not evolve toward resolution or cooperation; instead, it remains adversarial throughout, shaped by past betrayals and professional competition. The evidence is insufficient to confirm any underlying loyalty, respect, or camaraderie beneath the hostility.

memories.memory_text: The theater loomed above us, all brick and noise—so large, so vulgar. I could barely speak, only mutter that it was 'certainly... big,' as if words might betray how deeply it unsettled me.

I called 'Out!' when Essex slammed that shot, and though he glared, he said nothing. Then I asked Southampton how many had been at the play, and when he said two thousand, I calculated—five or six performances, ten thousand souls hearing one man’s words. That is power.

I stepped into the changing room just as Essex dismissed his valets, and saw them half-dressed, speaking in low tones—then I heard it: talk of intercepting Cecil’s letters, of denying James the throne, of backing a 'right' successor. I froze, unseen, and slipped away without a sound.
I warned Henry—the Cecils tolerate no rivals—and told him outright to deny Essex. He looked at me like I was clinging to old court games, but this is no game. Not with the throne at stake.
Just as he was mounting his horse, I called out—asked him to deliver a gift, an elaborate one. I didn’t explain, but the weight of it mattered. He agreed, though he didn’t know what he was carrying.

I stepped onto the stage in my winged costume, heart pounding, and spoke Puck’s lines just as we’d rehearsed—my voice clear in the great hall, and when I glanced to the side, my father’s face was lit with pride.
The applause came, and Young Elizabeth called 'Lovely! Lovely!'—but my eyes caught the stern man in black a few seats away, frowning deeply, his disapproval like a cold draft in the warm hall.

I felt the weight of silence when she entered—then her voice, bright and sudden: 'Compose something.' I did, on truth, and saw her smile, heard her clap. For the first time, a monarch named me a poet.

After I spoke of serving her in war and state, she teased Cecil about replacing him. I saw the tension between them, the way Cecil looked at my father—cold, unyielding. I smiled, but beneath it, I felt the first chill of court politics.
I told Jonson I secured his release by writing to the jailers in my father-in-law’s name—Lord William Cecil’s name carries weight, even when used without his blessing.
When Jonson asked if his freedom was officially sanctioned, I told him not to be an idiot—of course it wasn’t, but he’s free, isn’t he?

I told Jonson the truth—that I’ve written many plays, more than he’s likely ever seen, and that he would now put his name to all of them, not just one. I watched his face pale as the weight of it settled on him.

I left without a word, letting Francesco toss the coins at Jonson’s feet—payment and a threat wrapped in one. I didn’t look back, but I knew he was lost, both in the maze and in what I’d made him part of.

I greeted Master Crane in fluent French, then recited Plato in Greek when introduced to Mister Simmons—Boy Robert asked if it was Homer, and I corrected him sharply; the boy frowned, but I wouldn’t let ignorance pass.
I asked William Cecil about composition and poetry, and he said it was a sin in his Puritan household—his voice firm, his face unmoved, as if beauty itself were blasphemy.
I walked into my room and saw the parchments scattered across my desk—my poetry exposed, pages missing. Someone had been here, rifling through my private writings.
I saw two feet beneath the tapestry, charged, and drove my sword through—it pierced him. His screams didn't stop, and I stood there, breathless, caught between horror and something darker.
I killed him because he was stealing my poems—my words, the only thing that was truly mine. When I said 'My poems are my soul!', I meant every syllable.
Cecil used my crime to corner me, demanding I marry his daughter to protect my head. I saw it then—the way he turned my blood on the floor into a contract signed in silence.
I watched from the shadows of my box as the Prologue spoke my words, and the audience leaned forward in silence—this play, unclaimed by any name, was mine, and no one below knew it but me.

I watched from my box as the audience rose in thunderous applause, spellbound by the words on stage—words I knew as my own—and for the first time, I felt a pride so deep it silenced the ghosts of doubt that always whisper in my ear.

Henry stood before me, breathless from his ride, asking for my blessing to follow Essex to Ireland—and I could not bring myself to give it. I saw the hurt in his eyes when I refused, but the words would not come.

I watched him on stage—Shakespeare—fingers stained with ink as if proof of authorship, bowing to thunderous applause, claiming my words as his own. When he stammered out 'my words,' I whispered in disbelief: 'An actor?!!'
The voices won’t stop—they come in my sleep, in the hall, at supper—only when I write them down does my mind grow quiet. I told Anne that, desperate for her to understand why I can’t stop.
She tore the parchment—my words—right from under my hand and ripped it apart, screaming why I must write, why I humiliate the family. I could only stare, as if I didn’t understand what had happened.

I watched from the shadows of my box as the actor spoke my words, shaping them for the crowd’s delight, while the women fluttered their lashes and the wits drank to the performance—none knowing they celebrated me.
I rode beside her across the bridge, the hooves of our horses tapping lightly on the wood—just the two of us, no voices but ours, no eyes upon us.
I remember the heat of the fire on my skin, the weight of her against me as we came together on the throne—her lips on mine, the velvet beneath us, the reckless silence after each moan.
I saw her smile fade the moment I mentioned the Netherlands—her eyes narrowed, her body tensed under the furs, and I knew I had crossed from lover to threat in a single word.

I stood in that cold chapel, my voice breaking as I demanded to know what Cecil had done—she wouldn’t see me, not once, not after everything—and when he simply said she was on Progress, he walked away as if I were nothing.

I heard him stammering about needing more money, using that pretentious word—'aggrandized'—as if dressing up a threat could make it respectable. When he implied he’d expose the truth, I felt the room tighten around me, though I showed nothing.

After Francesco moved to throw him out, I stopped him—silence was no longer an option. I looked at Shakespeare and asked simply, 'How much?' Then, before the shock could settle, I told Francesco to pay him, in Italian, so no one else would misunderstand my order.
Bessie told me the Queen had my child—her words hung in the air like smoke from the fire, and I could not speak, could not move, only stare into the dark space between us.
I turned and heard Robert Cecil say Essex would be executed—and then that my son would be too. The words struck me like a physical blow; I could feel the blood leave my face.
Cecil claimed I was Elizabeth’s secret son, raised as a noble to one day claim the throne—my whole life a calculated design. I went cold, my breath caught, unable to speak.

I was sitting by the river, snow falling, wrapped in a blanket, when Anne came up behind me and said, 'Sentence has been passed.' She smiled as she told me they would behead Southampton in a week—my son, to be killed by his own mother’s hand. Her voice was venomous, almost triumphant.
I knelt before her and said, 'Then take my head. In our son's stead,' knowing it was the only offering she might not refuse.
I told her, 'But only after my death! Only then!'—my final condition, my last gift to the realm, though she turned away without reply.

dialogue_exemplars: Never a voice in government. Never a sword raised in glorious battle. No immortal deeds for my heirs to know me by. (beat) Words, merely words, are to be my legacy... (beat) You alone watch my plays and know them as mine. When I hear the applause, the cheering, of the audience, all those hands clapping, they are celebrating... another man. But in that cacophony of sounds, I strained to hear the sound of two hands only. Yours.

Did you know, Jonson, that my family can trace its peerage farther back than any family in the kingdom? We fought at Crecy. At Bosworth Field. At Agincourt. (beat) I inherited my Earldom as one of the wealthiest men ever to breathe English air... and at last breath, I shall be one of the poorest.

I can't very well use my name, can I? I'm the seventeenth Earl of Oxford. The Lord Great Chamberlain of England, Viscount Bolebec, Lord Escales, Sandford and Badlesmere, etc, etc. No. I have a... reputation to protect. In my world, one does not write plays, Jonson. People like you do.
So! Ten thousand souls. All listening to the writings of one man-- the ideas of one man. That's power, Robert. And if there is one thing the Cecils understand, it's power.
You presumed to think? On my behalf? Whatever made you believe you had that prerogative?
I have made it my life to know the character of men, Jonson. I know you. You may have betrayed me, but you will never betray my words...
She will call for me. And while I am with her, you will come-- not with an army, not with swords, but with her loyal subjects. The cobblers, the tinkers, the bricklayers of London.
If I had known my absence would cause your grace so much... longing, I would have returned much-- much-- sooner.
A romantic tragedy. In iambic pentameter.

An ap mekhanes thes. Deus ex machina. Machine of the Gods.

Lord William Cecil. I have the questionable distinction of being married to his only daughter.

memories.memory_text: I hear 'Our Shakespeare, rise' called on the stage, but I do not appear. No manuscript of mine is known. My life is spoken of in questions.

I remember the sharp crack of the tennis ball hitting the wall, and then Oxford's voice cutting through the court—'Ten thousand souls... the ideas of one man.' My words—my plays—reaching that many? It made my chest tighten, not with pride, but with something heavier, like fear.
I laughed when Jonson said he came to London to change the world with words—rhyme changing the world? It sounded like poetry drunk on its own fumes.
I smiled as I asked Jonson how much the man had offered him, watching his face tighten—his pride stung, but the question lingered, and I knew it would eat at him.
I dipped my fingers into the inkwell, staining them dark, then grabbed the quill and tucked the parchment under my arm—proof in hand, I stepped forward.
I bowed on stage, the applause washing over me, and when I tried to speak, my voice stammered—'I, I... my words... their acting'—I could barely form the sentence, but I said it.

I was walking with Jonson on London Bridge, reading my own words—'From ancient grudge break to new mutiny'—and suddenly it hit me: the whole thing was in verse, every line, and I whispered, 'Incredible!! The whole bloody thing in verse?!' It felt like seeing my soul stitched together in ink.

I saw that blonde selling apples, and just like that, I launched into 'But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?'—performing full-bodied for her, watching her smile, then turned to Jonson and said I'd have no trouble parting barmaids' legs after that, though inside I was desperate when I cried out that I need to act, every inch of me.

I burst into the Mermaid's Tavern, heart racing—Henslowe wants 'Romeo' to run a fortnight, a full fortnight! I shouted for Billy to bring a round, my voice cracking with excitement, but no one answered at first.
I saw my name grow larger on each new playbill, until it loomed above the title—'William Shakespeare's Hamlet'—as if the theater itself now bore my name.
I bowed to roaring crowds after each performance, and when I looked up, I saw Jonson and the Mermaid's Wits watching me in stony silence—their faces dark with defeat.
I bowed to the thunderous applause, rain still falling on my face, feeling the weight of their eyes even as the sky opened up.
Hands reached up, grabbed me, pulled me onto their shoulders—I was lifted, carried out, drenched and disbelieving, as if borne by the storm itself.
I told Ben straight—this isn’t a request. I’m building my own theater, one that fits the scale of my work, and I’ll have my guineas, one way or another.
I stared him down when he accused me of killing Kit—I didn’t flinch, even as the dogs tore into the bear. I told him I’d have my money, no matter what.
I stood there holding my wig and nose, heart pounding, and stammered out that I needed more money—my voice cracked like a boy’s in a cathedral choir.
After Oxford stopped Francesco from throwing me out, I looked him in the eye and said it plain: 'Four hundred pounds. A year.' I could taste the power shift in the air.
I unfurled the parchment right there at the table, showing them the spear and falcon blazing in garish colors—my coat-of-arms, proof I’d finally earned my place among gentlemen.
Jonson pulled out a parchment and a quill, then thrust the quill at me, demanding I write. I said there was no ink and left.

I was with the whore on the straw bed when the door opened. Francesco came in, then Oxford, holding a manuscript. She screamed and pulled a sheet to cover herself. Oxford tossed the manuscript to me and said I had an epic poem published.

Oxford tossed me a heavy pouch of coins after I worried aloud about the cost of keeping actors ready, then said, 'You've had an epic poem published today.' I remember fumbling the manuscript, stunned—'Published? You mean like in a book?'—as if the words couldn't quite land.
I stepped out into the light, reading my lines aloud—'She sinketh down, still hanging by his neck'—and couldn't help but smile. 'Oh, I like this...'

I hear their voices rise in the Mermaid Tavern, toasting my name like a battle cry—'To Shakespeare! And villainy!'—though I stand unseen in the shadows outside, heart pounding, breath shallow, knowing Jonson heard it too.
Jonson names my play, 'The History of King Richard the Third,' in Pole's room, and says it portrays Richard as a hunchback.

I was fixing an actor’s doublet when Burbage came up beside me, breathless, saying they were turning away hundreds—people packed like sardines, every seat taken. When I peeked through the curtain, the sight of that heaving crowd made my pulse quicken, a roar in my ears like the sea.
I saw the crowd surge up, shouting 'A pox on Cecil!'—not at the actor, but at the name, as if it were blood they wanted, not lines.
Backstage, Burbage looked at me—just a glance—but I felt it like a hand on my shoulder, heavy with what we both knew: this was no longer just a play.
I turned to Burbage and shouted that we had to close the play—now—before it was too late, my voice cracking with urgency as the chants grew louder from the galleries.

I stood in the shadows beyond the chamber doors, heart pounding, as the Queen condemned Oxford—and named me—accusing our plays of fomenting rebellion; her voice cracked with fury, and I knew then she held me as guilty as him.
I whispered 'No, no, no, no' as I watched Southampton step out—alive, broken, but free—while I stayed hidden in the fog, unable to reach him.
I was adjusting a line in 'Much Ado' when Jonson burst in, shouting about palaces and Scotland, calling me a fraud and a murderer—his voice slurred, sword swinging, tankard still in hand.
He charged at me roaring, I sidestepped, turned, grabbed him by the throat—felt his breath hot and sour—and when we were face to face, I told him, 'You came to me, Ben,' then shoved him down.
I remember the weight of the folio placed in my hands, the scent of fresh ink and paper, and Jonson’s words beneath mine—his voice, once rival, now framing me for eternity.
